newsitem.title: FRANCE: Axa, UAP merger surprises market.
newsitem.headline: Axa, UAP merger surprises market.

text.p: An announcement on Tuesday by Axa and Union des Assurances de Paris (UAP) that they planned a merger surprised analysts, who said they are waiting to see how the two reorganise their businesses, particularly in France.
They noted the merger would give Axa access to the German market through UAP's German subsidiary Colonia AG.
"It gives Axa a good German business," UBS Phillips & Drew insurance analyst Andrew Goodwin said. "The question is what Axa and UAP together can do in France," he said.

On Friday, analysts said UAP would be an improbable fit for Axa, which has built a worldwide presence through its 1991 acquisition of Equitable Cos of the United States and purchase last year of a 51 percent stake in Australia's second largest life insurer, National Mutual.
"It does take Axa more back into Europe and more back into non-life," Goodwin said.
Besides access to Germany, however, the merger would also boost Axa's position in France, where it is the country's second biggest insurer behind UAP.
"Axa feels its home base is not as strong as it would like it to be," one analyst, who declined to be named, said.
He noted that UAP's insurance premiums worldwide were around 50 percent bigger than those of Axa.

"I am surprised that it has happened so quickly. On an industrial level, it seems reasonable. It will creae a fairly balanced group, with however a few overlaps in Europe, especially in France," Claudie Casimir, analysts at brokers Massonaud said.
All were in little doubt that it would be Axa which dominated the new merged company.
"It is clear that Axa is taking the lead," another analyst, who declined to be named, said.
Some said they were surprised that UAP would be willing to go along with the merger just after recovering from the weight of hefty property provisions.
UAP last month reported a seven percent rise in first-half profits to 860 million francs ($170.1 million) after a big 2.0 billion franc loss for 1995.
"Given the fact they seemed to have turned a corner, I would have thought they would stay with that improvement," one analyst said.
But the decision to merge with a fellow French company might head off a more aggressive takeover bid from elsewhere.
